input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through as a vapour. Two quantities are commonly used to characterise performance. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, a dimensionless quantity. In the tests described here, the feed was 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. Only one feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 2.1 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 240, although its flux fell 7% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, achieved a flux of 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 560, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, which makes direct comparisons of this kind relatively uncommon. Results of this kind are valuable precisely because the three quantities are reported side by side for the same membranes under the same conditions. A membrane chosen on flux alone would look different from one chosen on selectivity or on stability, and in practice the operator's priorities will determine which of these matters most for a given duty. The comparison is nevertheless confined to the feed composition and the duration actually tested, and it should not be extended to other feeds or to longer campaigns without further evidence of the same kind.
target: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless. The feed was 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2.1 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 240; its flux fell 7% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 560; its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The polymer membrane passes more mass and separates less; the zeolite membrane separates more and holds its flux. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison is limited to the one feed composition and the stated duration. The two membranes divide the reported quantities between them: the polymer leads on flux, the zeolite leads on separation factor and on stability. No single ranking follows from the figures without a weighting the abstract does not supply, because the quantities answer different questions: flux states the area a duty would need, the separation factor states the enrichment a pass achieves, and the change over the test states how long either figure can be relied on. The feed and the duration bound every figure in the comparison. A different feed composition would change the driving force across each membrane, and a longer test would extend the stability statement beyond the point where the present evidence stops. Within those bounds, the comparison states what each membrane did on the same feed over the same period. The abstract reports the two membranes on equal terms and leaves the choice between them to the duty.
